headline: Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? No. Don't get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom.

paragraphs.text: Wisconsin Republican Sen. Ron Johnson called Social Security a 'scam' and urged lawmakers to shut it down
Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi scheme is born of fraud and relies on a constant stream of new unwitting investors.
Fear can lead us to do and say unexpected things.

It can push us toward panic selling, drive us to make wild assumptions about the world, and sometimes force us to take a hard look at our own finances. We are especially prone to these impulses when we are looking for something or someone to blame.

Wisconsin Republican Sen. Ron Johnson, the chairman of the Committee on the Budget, on Wednesday took aim at Social Security ahead of a hearing on the subject, calling it a scam. "It's grotesque and at this point, there really is no way to fix Social Security," he said. "It is a Ponzi scheme."

Social Security is not a Ponzi scheme. A Ponzi scheme is born of fraud and relies on a stream of new unwitting investors who pay the returns promised to earlier ones. Social Security is a pay-as-you-go program established by federal law, in which payroll taxes fund benefits.

He isn't the only one who's frustrated with Social Security. Experts attribute an expected shortfall in Social Security to demographic factors - older workers retiring, with some claiming benefits early out of fear that the funds will run out.
Social Security is a pay-as-you-go program established by federal law.

Unless Congress acts, the combined trust funds will run out in 2034, covering just 83% of benefits. A new AARP report said: "The share of gross domestic product subject to Social Security's payroll tax, the program's primary income source, has fallen steadily over the past four decades."

The Social Security taxable maximum is $184,500 for 2026 and $192,300 for 2027, meaning earnings above those limits are not subject to Social Security payroll taxes. In other words, a growing share of national income is excluded, contributing to the expected shortfall in funds.

Like Johnson, a Moneyist reader also used the "P" word. "The thought of living to 100 terrifies me more than dying. For me, the biggest fraud is telling people to wait until 70 to retire just to maximize their Social Security benefits - as if that's the only factor worth considering."

They continued: "I grew up in the 1980s, and the advice to never count on Social Security is sounding more and more like a warning than a prediction. I fear there will be a run on Social Security similar to the bank runs before the Great Depression. Long live the Ponzi!"

Addressing the criticisms

The reader is essentially asking four questions: (1) Will fear trigger a Social Security crisis? (2) Is Social Security a Ponzi scheme? (3) Why sacrifice your 60s to get a bigger check at 70? And (4) Can you really count on Social Security?

(1) As for fear leading to a crisis: Probably not, so do not get carried away with 1930s-era prophecies of doom and gloom. A run on a bank involves a large number of people withdrawing their money and, if the bank cannot meet those withdrawals, even an otherwise solvent institution can fail.

I grew up in the 1980s too, and here's a fun fact about Generation X: The American Institute of Stress says we are apparently more stressed out than other generations. The main reason for that, researchers theorize, is that we are worried about falling short on our retirement goals.

(2) Social Security is a social-insurance program funded by workers and employers to provide support in retirement, prevent vulnerable people from falling into poverty and provide economic stability during downturns. It is at risk of a shortfall in funding, not annihilation.
Social Security is at risk of a shortfall in funding, not annihilation.

(3) You can claim Social Security at 62, but doing so reduces your monthly benefit by 30% compared with waiting until your full retirement age (FRA) of 67. Waiting until 70 increases your benefit by 8% for each year you delay beyond 67. That's 24% more in total.

If you are collecting Social Security and remain below FRA throughout 2026, you can earn up to $24,480 before benefits are withheld. Above that limit, $1 is withheld for every $2 you earn. At FRA, Social Security recalculates your benefit to account for withholdings.

Yes, some people do claim Social Security benefits early due to fears about the program's long-term viability. But the program values stability, security and peace of mind over recklessness, madcap investments and promises of riches.

(4) You can count on Social Security, which is not projected to disappear. Payroll taxes and other incoming revenue will keep funding benefits. Under current projections, though, that revenue would cover only 83% of scheduled benefits from the combined trust funds in 2034.

Why we have Social Security

Social Security was created in 1935 in response to the Great Depression and was not intended to maximize investment returns. Today, it provides a social safety net against the financial hardships of retirement, disability and the loss of a family's breadwinner.

There are two separate funds: the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund and the Disability Insurance Trust Fund. Their reserves are invested in special-issue U.S. Treasury securities, backed by the full faith and credit of the federal government.

So what about this looming funding crisis? The Congressional Budget Office said earlier this year that the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which pays retirement and survivors benefits, is projected to run out of reserves in 2032.

The Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, said in a June report that, at that point, incoming revenue would cover just 78% of scheduled benefits from that fund. Without congressional action, those shortfalls would mean across-the-board reductions in benefits.
There is already a demographic 'run' on Social Security.

"The program's long-run outlook worsened significantly this year," it said. "The Social Security Administration (SSA) revised its fertility and immigration projections downward." The 75-year shortfall has risen to approximately $30 trillion - up from $26 trillion last year.

There is already a demographic "run" on Social Security. The Bipartisan Policy Center said "an aging population is a major contributor to the problem." The ratio of workers to beneficiaries has dropped from 5-to-1 in 1960 to 2.6-to-1 in 2025 and is projected to fall to 1.9-to-1 by 2075.

The Social Security Disability Insurance Trust Fund is projected to remain solvent until 2100, the end of the Board of Trustees' 75-year projection period, but the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, under current estimates, won't have enough to pay full benefits in 2032.

We are encouraged to delay our dream life, save more, work longer and maximize our retirement contributions. Still, the price of financial security should not be spending our 60s worrying about our 70s, 80s and 90s, and beyond. For millions of people, however, that worry is a daily reality.
Keep calm and carry on working, if you can, and saving for retirement.
